title: Building Networks for Marriage
author: Michael Foster
summary: Foster addresses how tight theological circles, geographic isolation, and narrow non-negotiable lists create courtship bottlenecks for young adults. He argues Reformed and conservative families often make compounding narrowing decisions without maintaining sufficiently broad networks. The solution: deliberate networking across compatible churches, travel for conferences, extended visits, and involvement in broader communities. Foster emphasizes that generational thinking applies to networks, not just land; without people, homesteads don't build lineages. Meeting online is now statistically primary but shouldn't replace in-person community and mutual accountability.
points: Ultra-narrow choices: tight theology + remote geography + ideological filters create courtship crises
Requires near-perfect execution; most families can't sustain such high-difficulty settings
Solution: broader relational web across compatible churches, travel for opportunity
Generational thinking applies to networks as much as homesteads; need both
Online meeting now primary channel (50% statistically) but in-person networks still vital
quotes: A lot of Reformed families have accidentally engineered a bottleneck for their own kids.
If you make five or six compounding narrowing decisions, you shouldn't be surprised when outcomes narrow too.
Land without people doesn't build a lineage. You need both.
If you want your kids to marry well, you have to put them in the path of good options.

Conviction is good. Isolation isn't. If you want a generational future, you have to cultivate a generational network, not just a generational homestead.” Archived from This is Foster on May 2, 2026 by Tim.
